summary:
Galicia stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023 (BOE-A-2023-5366), on real and effective equality for trans persons and the guarantee of LGBTI rights. Title II of the law regulates rectification of the registered sex entry by the person's freely expressed will. The procedure is depathologised: no medical diagnosis or treatment is required, the former age-majority requirement for filing has been removed, and identity documents are adapted accordingly. Title III provides protection and reparation against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence.

Article 43 allows any person aged 16 or over to request rectification directly before the Civil Registry. Recognition is available from age 12 under stated conditions, a provision that provoked political conflict when the law was passed. Human Rights Watch recorded the reform as replacing the prior requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment aligned to the sought marker with self-identification through a simple administrative process, and assessed it as upholding European and international standards against abusive and disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

Implementation of the education-facing and administrative provisions sits with the autonomous communities, the Galician government among them, alongside the health and workplace measures the statute mandates across administrative, workplace, health and education fields. The law also bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before their consent, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthens sexuality education, and prohibits discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime in Spain: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo, in the province of Pontevedra, applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force in Spain since 2005, and legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.
tangentialFactors:
Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change; the survey predates Ley 4/2023 and functions as a dated baseline rather than a current measure.

Provisions adjacent to gender recognition sit in the same statute: expanded assisted reproduction rules, strengthened sexuality education in schools, and a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children. These do not bear directly on a visitor's entry, documentation or movement, but they shape the clinical and educational environment a trans or intersex traveller would encounter in Galician facilities.

Human Rights Watch framed the 2023 reform as a victory in the fight for gender recognition, an advocacy assessment rather than a judicial finding; the operative authority for the requirements stated above is the gazetted text of Ley 4/2023 itself.
localsOnly:
Residents of Galicia obtain rectification of the registered sex entry directly before the Civil Registry under Article 43, without a diagnosis, treatment or surgical prerequisite, and their identity documents follow the corrected entry. Legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

The Galician government, as an autonomous community, implements the law's education-facing and administrative provisions, including the anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing and the strengthened sexuality education curriculum.

For minors, recognition is available from age 12 under conditions set by the statute, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16. Non-consensual normalising surgery on intersex children is banned.

Protection against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence falls under Title III of Ley 4/2023, with the transfobia aggravating circumstance available to prosecutors and courts; the Vigo decision of July 2026 confirms its application at first-instance level.

Unmarried same-sex couples benefit from parental recognition provisions, and same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Galician regional statute or implementing decree of Ley 4/2023 is cited in the source inventory, so the specific instruments through which the Galician government executes the education and administrative provisions remain unresolved.

Processing times, fee schedules, refusal rates and appeal routes for Civil Registry filings in Galicia are not sourced here; the inventory establishes the legal entitlement and the age thresholds only.

The sources do not document trans-specific violence in Galicia beyond the Vigo misdemeanour case of July 2026, nor whether Galician authorities have published guidance on sex-separated facilities applying the legal-gender basis.

Whether the transfobia aggravating circumstance has been applied in Galicia in cases beyond the Vigo decision, and how the Article 510 hate-speech penalties have been enforced regionally, are not evidenced in the inventory.
